Simplified supply chain diagram for mg-Si 40 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.7.1 Technology Trends for Metallurgical-Grade Silicon Most mg-Si is produced through carbothermic reduction of silica sand (silicon dioxide) into mg- Si and carbon dioxide in a submerged electric arc furnace (EAF). The silica sand is a high-purity, low-iron, low-boron quartz sand. Advances have been made in the efficiency of the EAFs, reducing energy demands from over 35 kWh/kg to less than 13 kWh/kg (Chen et al. 2018, 2017, 2016; Mirletz et al. 2024). Alternatives to the EAF include hydrogen reduction and using metals as alternate reductants, but none of these are commercially viable (Hoover et al. 2024). Multiple non-PV applications—including silicones, silanes, other semiconductors, and aluminum alloys—also use mg-Si. Different applications have different purity requirements, and specific mg-Si manufacturing approaches are not necessarily substitutable to another application. Many facilities tune their process to a known incoming material stream and impurity profile, increasing the barrier to substitution. 2.7.2 Domestic Production of Metallurgical-Grade Silicon In 2024, mg-Si was produced in the United States by three companies: Ferroglobe, Dow Chemical, and Mississippi Silicon. Dow Chemical and Mississippi Silicon are U.S. companies, while Ferroglobe is headquartered in the United Kingdom. Table 5 and Figure 28 list U.S. facilities, including those producing mg-Si for non-PV applications. In 2024, U.S. mg-Si production capacity for PV polysilicon was about 74 kt/yr, out of 190 kt/yr of total U.S. capacity. The 74 kt/yr could serve 35.7 GW /yr of polysilicon production,30 dc significantly exceeding mg-Si demand from domestic polysilicon producers. Table 5.
